_note: Every visible string of a statement page's Lean file view and its 'What you must check' panel (scripts/lean_render.py). Placeholders in braces are filled from data. Plain words; no em dashes.

file.heading: The complete Lean statement file
file.intro: {lines} lines, copied from release version {commit}. A name defined in this file links to its line; pointing at the name shows its definition.
file.legend_mathlib: Other linked names open the current documentation for Mathlib, Lean’s mathematical library.
file.counts: Links in the file: {local} to its own declarations, {ext} to Mathlib’s documentation.

counts_imported.one: {n} more goes to the OpenAI modules the file imports.
counts_imported.many: {n} more go to the OpenAI modules the file imports.

counts_library.one: {n} declared name also links to the same declaration in OpenAI’s library.
counts_library.many: {n} declared names also link to the same declaration in OpenAI’s library.

counts_plain.one: {n} identifier stays plain because it resolves to no single declaration: a variable Lean binds automatically, notation, or a name the scan of the pinned sources did not find.
counts_plain.many: {n} identifiers stay plain because they resolve to no single declaration: variables Lean binds automatically, notation, or names the scan of the pinned sources did not find.

counts_ambiguous.one: {n} of them could name more than one declaration.
counts_ambiguous.many: {n} of them could name more than one declaration.

file.namespace_note: Names in the namespace {ns} are listed without it.
file.mathlib_note: OpenAI uses Mathlib version {mathlib}. The linked documentation describes the current version, so names that have since changed may be missing there.

panel.heading: Definitions and lemmas named by the statement
panel.intro: If Comparator accepts a proof, it proves {theorem} exactly as written here. To compare that statement with the paper, also read the definitions and lemmas listed below. Atlas found them by following names in the source text and lists each after the names it uses. For x.foo, Atlas includes every foo defined here for a type, even when the statement may use only one of them.

summary.one: It reaches {n} of the file’s {total} other declarations; with the theorem itself they span {lines} lines.
summary.many: It reaches {n} of the file’s {total} other declarations; with the theorem itself they span {lines} lines.

panel.intro_holes: The verification settings name no theorem. Comparator instead tests whether OpenAI’s library defines {names} with the types written here. The list below follows names used by those definitions; each appears after the names it uses.
panel.holes_note: For a definition marked “name and type only”, Comparator does not compare the definition’s body with the one here. It verifies the proof using the definition in OpenAI’s library. Follow the library link to compare the two definitions.

summary_all.one: It reaches the file’s only other declaration; with the theorem itself they span {lines} lines.
summary_all.many: It reaches all {n} other declarations of the file; with the theorem itself they span {lines} lines.

panel.summary_none: The statement reaches no other declaration of this file.

summary_imported.one: It also names {n} declaration from the OpenAI modules the file imports, listed below.
summary_imported.many: It also names {n} declarations from the OpenAI modules the file imports, listed below.

panel.imported_heading: Definitions and lemmas from other OpenAI files
panel.imported_intro: The statement also names these definitions or lemmas in OpenAI’s library. The links open the version of the library used by this release.

summary_direct.one: {n} of them is named in the statement itself.
summary_direct.many: {n} of them are named in the statement itself.

panel.rel_aria: Show what {name} uses and what uses it
panel.implicit_heading: Other Lean rules that may affect the statement
panel.implicit_intro: Lean can use instances, notation and attributes without naming them in the statement. These are rules for interpreting or finding mathematical objects. Atlas’s scan of names cannot follow all such uses; read the listed source as well.

not_needed.one: {n} declaration the statement does not reach by name
not_needed.many: {n} declarations the statement does not reach by name

panel.not_needed_intro: These definitions and lemmas were not found by following names in the statement. Lean may still use them through rules such as instances or macros.

script.card_library: The same declaration in OpenAI’s library at {commit}

page.readings_link: Read the complete assessments on the family page.

page.report_check: Report a comparison with the paper (GitHub issue)
page.intro: Lean is a language for mathematical statements and proofs that a computer can verify. This page shows one statement file from OpenAI’s release, possible paper matches and independent reports. The code-like names below identify the definitions or theorems selected by the proof-verification settings.

pairing.cited_how: A source comment for {declaration} names this theorem’s label in the paper’s TeX source.
pairing.cited_link: Read the source comment from line {line}
pairing.join_label: How the paper theorem and the Lean statement are linked
pairing.assoc_unresolved: The Lean source cites labels that do not resolve to a single theorem, so no theorem is paired.
pairing.no_record: Atlas’s source records list no possible paper match for this Lean statement.
pairing.no_confident: no paper statement matches the Lean text clearly enough to pair, so the closest candidates are listed below.
pairing.how_lean: Words of the Lean statement, its names split into words, that also appear in the theorem: {words}.
pairing.how_title: Found in the paper’s title, which its main theorem states: {words}.
pairing.how_note: Shared only with the release’s name for the Lean statement or OpenAI’s note on it: {words}.
pairing.how_catalogue: Shared with the catalogue’s wording or OpenAI’s note, none of them matched in the Lean text: {words}.
pairing.how_nothing: It shares no telling word with the Lean text; it is listed as the next nearest statement.

evidence.lean-words: Atlas selected this possible match by comparing words in the Lean statement with every statement in the family. No review of whether the statements mean the same thing is recorded.
evidence.catalogue-words: No paper statement clearly matched the Lean wording. Statement Map, the program that collects Atlas’s source records, selected this possible match using words in OpenAI’s catalogue and Lean note. No review of whether the statements mean the same thing is recorded.
evidence.lean-words-multi: Atlas selected possible matches by comparing words in each part of the Lean statement with every statement in the family. No review of whether the statements mean the same thing is recorded.

paper_why.listed: Statements in {paper} come first because the release lists only that paper for this Lean statement.
paper_why.label: Statements in {paper} come first because the release’s name for this Lean statement shares words with that paper’s title.
paper_why.files: Statements in {paper} come first because the Lean file and module names share words with that paper’s title.
paper_why.draft: Statements in {paper} come first because the AI draft reading of OpenAI’s note shares words with that paper’s title.

pairing.multi_intro: The Lean statement joins several assertions with “and”. Atlas selected possible matches to {n} paper results from their shared wording, listed below. This does not establish that their mathematical meanings agree.
pairing.method: How Atlas selects possible matches: it compares words in the Lean statement with every statement in the family. It also splits Lean names into words. The release’s label and note receive less weight; a main theorem wins a close match. If the Lean wording yields no clear match, Atlas uses the catalogue description. This selects passages to compare; it does not establish that they mean the same thing.

runs.pin_current: at the release version shown here
runs.pin_other: at version {pin}, which differs from the release version shown here
runs.method: How they ran it, in their words
runs.reported: Each group reports its own Comparator run for this statement file. Atlas has not repeated the runs.
runs.none_recorded: Atlas has no report of an independent group running Comparator for this statement.
runs.scope: For a configured theorem, Comparator tests whether OpenAI’s proof proves the exact Lean statement. Some files instead configure definitions for comparison by name and type. Acceptance does not establish that the statement means the same thing as the paper’s theorem.

readings.defs: Definitions the group asks readers to compare with the paper:

card.reruns_one: One independent group reports that Comparator accepted a run for this file at the release version shown here.
card.reruns_many: {n} independent groups report that Comparator accepted runs for this file at the release version shown here.

table.lede: Lean is a language for mathematical statements and proofs that a computer can verify. The release supplies {lean} statement files, listing {main} as main results. Each row links a Lean statement to its possible paper counterpart and shows independent assessments and reports of proof verification.
table.caption: Lean statements, possible paper matches, independent assessments of each family and reports of accepted Comparator runs

pair.catalogue-words: possible match from catalogue wording; no review recorded

table.note_holes_many: {n} definitions checked by name and type only
table.none_match: No Lean statement matches these filters.
